name: 銀座 篝 本店
cuisine: The chicken-paitan ramen shop Ginza queues for — a thick, almost potage-textured 鶏白湯 SOBA over medium-thin straight noodles, topped with sous-vide chicken breast and a fan of seasonal vegetables; ¥1,200 for the plain bowl up to about ¥2,500 for the fresh-truffle version, with a clam-and-oyster shio soba and a chicken-and-porcini tsuke-soba alongside. Buy a ticket at the machine (cashless), then queue.
neighborhood: Ginza 6-chōme, in the narrow lane one street back from Dentsū-dōri, side by side with sister shop Ginza Oborozuki — 2 min from Ginza Station exit C2 (Ginza / Marunouchi / Hibiya lines)
gf_detail: Wheat from end to end and no gluten-free claim anywhere. The noodles are Mikawaya Seimen wheat noodles; the brand's own retail version of the signature bowl lists めん（小麦粉…）and しょうゆ in the soup, with the statutory allergen line 「一部に乳成分・小麦・大豆・鶏肉を含む」. The kaeshi is ordinary wheat shōyu. Nothing here is workable for a celiac.
vegan_detail: The whole point of the shop is chicken: the broth is chicken carcasses and whole birds boiled for hours in nothing but water, and the topping is chicken chāshū. The tsuke version adds pork chāshū, the shio version clams and oysters. No vegan or vegetarian bowl is published.

roles: independent Ginza ramen house, part of a small group with 銀座 朧月 and 蝋燭屋
chef_bio.background: Kagari built its name on 鶏白湯 — chicken paitan — at a time when Ginza had almost no serious ramen, and it is now one of the most internationally famous ramen counters in Tokyo. The operation's own copy describes the soup as 国産銘柄鶏100% chicken carcasses and whole birds simmered for a long time in pure water alone, giving a rich but clean, sediment-free broth, and it sells a five-portion retail kit of the signature 鶏白湯Soba through its own BASE shop. The shop has moved within Ginza — a long-standing reviewer records a twelve-year gap between visits and notes the relocation — and now sits in a back lane beside its sister shop Oborozuki, 18 seats in a コの字 counter of 14 plus a wall counter of 4, with about six cooks working flat out. The group also runs 蝋燭屋 (a Sichuan-pepper 汁なし担々麺 shop) and a 大手町 branch of Kagari. No individual owner-chef is named on the shop's own pages.
chef_bio.philosophy: Ramen priced and plated for Ginza: a French-leaning chicken potage of a soup, truffle oil and Wakayama budō-sanshō oil sold as part of the experience, vegetables arranged for colour.
chef_bio.specialty: 鶏白湯Soba and 特製鶏白湯Soba; the fresh-truffle 特製 鶏白湯醤油Soba; 蛤と牡蠣Soba; 鶏とポルチーニ茸の醤油つけSoba; a chicken-chāshū butter rice with truffle shōyu.

anecdotes.text: The queue is famously almost all overseas visitors — one Japanese reviewer writes that between the foreign customers in line and the foreign staff at the door 「自分がいったいどこに来たのかわからなくなりました」. A greeter hands out menus in English on the pavement and walks you to the ticket machine.
Regulars note the two-tier reality of the lane: Kagari with 7 people waiting, nearly all inbound tourists, and Oborozuki next door with 14, nearly all Japanese.
Pricing has moved sharply upmarket — several 2025–2026 reviews record the standard bowl at ¥2,000 and the truffle bowl at ¥2,400, well above the ¥1,200 shown on older menu listings.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog's page for 銀座 篝 本店 carries the address 東京都中央区銀座6-4-12 1F, the coordinates used here, a 3.66 aggregate over 1,565 reviews, and the review body quoted above. The group's own BASE shop carries the description of the broth (国産銘柄鶏100%, 鶏ガラと丸鶏, 純水で長時間) and the full statutory ingredient and allergen listing for the retail set. Yahoo's business card confirms 11:00–21:30 daily, 定休日 不定休, and the phone number 03-6263-8900.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A single small kitchen boiling wheat noodles continuously for an 18-seat counter turning over every ten minutes. There is no separate pot and no gluten-free line.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The retail version of the house bowl lists しょうゆ in the soup and declares 小麦 and 大豆 among its allergens; the shop-made kaeshi is ordinary wheat shōyu. No tamari is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is chicken carcasses and whole birds; toppings include chicken and pork chāshū and, in one bowl, clams and oysters. Everything comes out of the same stock pot.

positives.text: Fully published ingredient and allergen list for the retail version of the signature bowl — unusual transparency for a ramen shop, even if the answer is 'wheat'.

cultural_comfort.note: Probably the easiest door in Ginza for a non-Japanese speaker: a greeter with fluent English hands you a menu in the queue, walks you to the ticket machine and presses the buttons, and payment is cashless card-tap. Reviewers repeatedly note that most of the room and much of the staff are non-Japanese. The trade-off is Ginza-tourist pricing and a wait that can run to an hour on a Saturday evening; arriving before noon or mid-afternoon cuts it to ten minutes.

enrich_note: CUISINE CORRECTION. The light record's name was right but its cuisine was not: it read 「Yakitori」, and 銀座 篝 is a chicken-paitan ramen counter, not a yakitori house. Business confirmed via Tabelog (13230021) and the operator's own BASE shop; address 中央区銀座6-4-12 1F, phone 03-6263-8900, and coordinates taken from Tabelog's map data, so the neighbourhood-centroid pin has been replaced with the real one (about 400 m south-west of the old approximate pin). Gluten and vegan tiers are both 'no' on published ingredient evidence, not inference.

name: 竹葉亭 銀座店
cuisine: A hundred-year-plus unagi house a minute from the Ginza crossing, on three floors — basement and ground-floor chairs, tatami upstairs. Charcoal-grilled kabayaki over rice (鰻丼 ¥3,200, うな重 ¥3,960–¥4,950), the liver soup at ¥300, and the house's other famous dish, 鯛茶漬 sea bream over rice with tea poured on, at ¥1,800–¥2,450, plus うざく and うまき玉子 to drink with. No reservations — you turn up and wait.
neighborhood: Ginza 5-chōme, on the Ginza Core side of the crossing — 1 min from Ginza Station exit A5 (Ginza line), 6 min from JR Yūrakuchō
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim, and the wheat is in the sauce rather than at the edge of the plate. Kabayaki is built on a tare of wheat shōyu and mirin brushed on repeatedly over the coals, and the 鯛茶漬 sits in a sesame-and-soy dressing before the tea goes on. うまき玉子 (egg rolled round eel) and うざく (eel with cucumber in vinegar) both carry soy as well. Nothing on the menu is made with a gluten-free tamari.
vegan_detail: A specialist eel restaurant: eel, sea bream, egg, and a bonito-and-eel-bone stock behind the soups. There is no vegetable course and no vegan or vegetarian option published on the shop's own page or in its menu listing.

roles: 長寿の老舗うなぎ屋 (long-established eel house); the Ginza branch of the Chikuyōtei house
chef_bio.origin: Founded in the closing years of the Edo period at 東京あさり河岸 — the Asari riverbank, what is now Shintomichō in Chūō-ku, a few hundred metres from where the Ginza shop stands today
chef_bio.background: Chikuyōtei was founded at the end of the Edo period on the Asari riverbank in what is now Shintomichō, and its own house history records that it was loved by generations of 文人墨客 — the writers and painters of Meiji and Taishō Tokyo. It spread to the Kansai only when businessmen of the calibre of Kobayashi Ichizō, the founder of Hankyū, and Itō Chūbei of the Itōchū house invited it there in the early Shōwa years; those invitations produced the Osaka and Nagoya branches that still trade. The Ginza shop is the everyday face of the house rather than a special-occasion room: its own page bills itself simply as 「100年以上続くうなぎ料理の老舗『竹葉亭』の味をお気軽にご賞味下さい」 — come and try the old shop's cooking without ceremony — and points out that its 鯛茶漬け is as celebrated as the eel. Sixty seats over three levels, tatami rooms included, entirely non-smoking, cards accepted, no parking, and famously no reservations at all: 「お席のご予約は承っておりません」.
chef_bio.philosophy: An old Edo eel house run as a walk-in restaurant rather than a reservation-only one — the same kabayaki and the same 鯛茶漬け that fed Meiji Tokyo, served at a price a Ginza office worker can pay at lunch.

anecdotes.text: The house's own history credits Kobayashi Ichizō and Itō Chūbei with drawing Chikuyōtei out of Tokyo — the Kansai branches exist because those two invited the Tokyo shop west in the early Shōwa years.

The Ginza shop takes no bookings of any kind and says so in block capitals on its own page; a reviewer arriving five minutes before the 11:30 opening on a weekday found seven or eight parties already in line.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own official page (gnavi-hosted, g201101.gorp.jp) supplies the address 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座5-8-3, the phone number 03-3571-0677, the structured coordinates used here, the full weekday/weekend opening hours with last orders, the 第1・第3月曜日 closure with its holiday rule, 60 seats with tatami, wholly non-smoking, six card brands accepted, no parking, English and simplified-Chinese menus, and a children-not-admitted policy. 東京竹葉亭's corporate site carries the founding history. Yahoo's business card and Tabelog (13002552) independently confirm the address, hours, closure days and the priced menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A 60-seat eel kitchen with no allergen programme published. The tare pot is shared across every grilled dish and the same sauce goes on the rice.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kabayaki tare is wheat shōyu and mirin; the 鯛茶漬け dressing is soy and sesame. No gluten-free tamari is offered or mentioned anywhere on the shop's own page or its menu listing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every dish on the card is eel, sea bream or egg. There is no vegetable dish to build a meal from.

positives.text: Menus are available in English and simplified Chinese, so at least the ingredients can be read before ordering.

cultural_comfort.note: A walk-in old shop, one minute from Ginza exit A5, with English and simplified-Chinese menus and six card brands accepted; the whole building is non-smoking. Two things to know before you go: it takes no reservations at all, so arrive at 11:30 or expect to queue, and its own page states 「お子様連れNG」 — children are not admitted. Ask for the 鯛茶漬け if the eel price is too steep; it is the dish regulars order.

name: てんぷら 近藤
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座5-5-13 坂口ビル9F
cuisine: Two-Michelin-star Edomae tempura on the ninth floor of a Ginza building, twenty seats across two counters, with Kondō Fumio himself frying at both services. Course only: lunch 菫 ¥13,200 / 椿 ¥16,500, dinner 藤 ¥22,000 / 楓 ¥27,500 / 蓬 ¥33,000, tax included. The batter is pared as thin as it will hold, and the vegetables — above all a stump-thick block of sweet potato fried slowly for half an hour — are the reason to come.
neighborhood: Ginza 5-chōme, ninth floor of the Sakaguchi Building — 1 min from Ginza Station exit B5, about 5 min from the Ginza / Marunouchi / Hibiya line concourse
gf_detail: Wheat is the technique here, not a contaminant. The restaurant's own copy opens with 「小麦粉で作る天ぷらの衣」 — the batter is wheat flour, and the entire argument of the house is about how thin that wheat coat can be made. Tentsuyu is a bonito dashi cut with wheat shōyu. There is no gluten-free claim and no wheat-free preparation; a celiac cannot eat a tempura course.
vegan_detail: Vegetables are Kondō's signature — he says outright that he brought them into high-end tempura because Edomae tempura had been seafood-only and he wanted a course that could stand beside Japanese or French cooking — but the courses themselves are seafood-and-vegetable, one pot of oil fries the prawns and the sweet potato alike, and the dipping sauce is a bonito dashi. Nothing vegan is offered on the published menu.

chef_bio.background: Kondō joined the celebrated tempura kitchen of Yamanoue — 「てんぷらと和食 山の上」, the restaurant of the Hilltop Hotel in Kanda — straight out of high school, was handed the head chef's job at twenty-three, and ran that kitchen for more than twenty years before going independent in 1991 and opening Tempura Kondō in Ginza. His argument is that tempura is not really deep-frying at all but steaming: the batter seals the ingredient, the residual heat after it leaves the oil finishes the cooking, and the frying has to be timed for that carry-over or the dish fails. From that follows the batter he is known for — pared to the thinnest coat that will hold, so it takes up almost no oil and lets the colour and smell of the ingredient through. His second and larger contribution was vegetables: Edomae tempura had been seafood, with fried vegetables treated as delicatessen food unworthy of a serious restaurant, and Kondō decided that a cuisine meaning to stand with Japanese and French cooking had to use the vegetables of its own place. He contracts for produce only after tasting it where it grows, asking growers for 「本当のもの、最高のもの」. The signature is a block of sweet potato over ten centimetres thick, fried slowly for about thirty minutes so the water and the sugar stay sealed inside. He was the first tempura cook ever named a 現代の名工 (Contemporary Master Craftsman, an honour conferred by Japan's Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare) in 2019, and the first tempura cook to take the Michelin Guide's Mentor Chef Award, in the Tokyo 2024 guide. The restaurant has held two Michelin stars continuously since 2008. Past fifty years at the fryer, he still stands at the counter for both services on the principle that 「天ぷらは、料理人がゲストをお招きする料理」 — tempura is a dish in which the cook is the host.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tempura as a steamed dish rather than a fried one; the thinnest wheat coat that will hold; and vegetables raised to the centre of a cuisine that had treated them as an afterthought.
chef_bio.specialty: The thirty-minute whole sweet potato (さつまいも, also listed à la carte at ¥1,200); the vegetable-led courses 菫 and 椿 at lunch and 藤・楓・蓬 at dinner.

anecdotes.text: Kondō's own account of the sweet potato: 「さつまいもって焼きいもにするとおいしいじゃない？　だから焼きいもに勝る味を天ぷらで出そうと考え出来たのが、今のさつまいもの天ぷらです」 — a roast sweet potato is delicious, so he set out to beat it with tempura.
He was made head chef of the Yamanoue tempura kitchen at twenty-three and stayed more than twenty years before opening his own place at forty-four.
The room is two counters only — one of twelve seats and one of eight — and services run on fixed start times with a strict two- or two-and-a-half-hour limit.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The restaurant's own site carries Kondō's biography (born 1947, Yamanoue from eighteen, head chef at twenty-three, independent 1991), the awards with their dates (現代の名工 2019, Mentor Chef Award in the Tokyo 2024 guide, two Michelin stars every year since 2008), his stated method (tempura as steaming, thin wheat batter, vegetables), the address 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座5-5-13 坂口ビル9F, phone 03-5568-0923, the Sunday closure, both the current and the September-2026 revised service times, the seat count and the full priced course list. Yahoo's business card independently confirms the address, the Ginza exit B5 walk and the service window.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Every course is battered in wheat flour and fried in one shared pot of oil. There is no wheat-free item on the card and no separate fryer.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tentsuyu is a bonito dashi seasoned with ordinary wheat shōyu; no tamari is mentioned. Salt and lemon are offered alongside, but that does not help when the coating itself is wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The vegetables that made the restaurant's name are fried in the same oil as the prawns and fish, and dipped in a bonito dashi.

positives.text: Overseas guests are handled through an official multilingual booking desk (My Concierge Japan) with English, traditional and simplified Chinese and Korean forms, so a dietary question can at least be raised in writing before the meal.

cultural_comfort.note: A counter of twenty on a ninth floor, course-only, with fixed start times and a hard two-hour limit — this is a booking, not a walk-in. Phone reservations are Japanese only and the restaurant says so plainly; overseas guests are routed to My Concierge Japan, which takes bookings in English, Chinese and Korean, and the site itself runs in five languages. Once you are seated the format carries you: pieces come one at a time from the fryer in front of you, and salt or lemon means you need very little Japanese to eat well. Closed Sundays, and on the Monday when Monday is a public holiday.

enrich_note: Confirmed, with a location correction. The light record filed 天ぷら 近藤 as 「築地駅 徒歩（中央区）」 and pinned it on the Tsukiji centroid; the restaurant is in Ginza, 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座5-5-13 坂口ビル9F — same ward, but about 800 m away and served by Ginza Station exit B5, not Tsukiji. Identity, address, phone (03-5568-0923), hours, prices and the chef's biography all come from the restaurant's own site, cross-checked against Yahoo's business card. Coordinates are the street address geocoded through the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan's address-search service, so they are the building's lot rather than a surveyed shop door. Gluten 'no' is not an assumption: the house's own opening line of copy is 「小麦粉で作る天ぷらの衣」.

chef_bio.background: Amazake-yokochō is a real place, but it is a street, not a business. It is the shopping lane that runs from Ningyōchō Station towards Hamachō and the Meijiza theatre, named for the sweet-sake stall that once stood at its mouth, and it is administered by a shotengai association whose own site (amazakeyokocho.jp) organises its members into four categories — 名物食品処, ご飲食とお酒処, 装い処 and 匠の店・ベターライフ — and describes the street as 「老舗名店の連なる情緒あふれた下町の散歩道」. Tokyo's official tourism board describes it the same way: a small shopping street cutting through Nihonbashi, lined with traditional confectioners and old-style Japanese restaurants. The association still runs street events — 「甘酒横丁 ちょっと夜ふかし」 falls on 22 August 2026, held alongside the Ōedo bon-odori in Hamachō Park. Named traders on it include とうふの双葉, the tofu maker founded in 1907 that sells the amazake the street is named for. A single app record covering 'various vendors' cannot represent any of them.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shotengai association's own site gives the street's extent (中央区日本橋人形町／浜町), its member categories and its 2026 event calendar. Yahoo's place card gives 人形町駅 A2 徒歩0分, the association phone number 03-3666-7662 and the explicit hours note 「店舗により異なる」. GO TOKYO, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government's official travel site, describes the street's origin in the amazake stall at its entrance.

cultural_comfort.note: As a walk it could not be easier — it starts at exit A2 of Ningyōchō Station and takes ten minutes end to end, and browsing is expected. But it is a street, and this record cannot tell a traveller which door to open, when it is open or what it will feed them. If the street is worth keeping in the app it should be re-entered as individual shops (とうふの双葉 for the amazake, and so on), not as one composite pin.
